lesson.title: Pulling the Common Factor Out Front: Factoring by GCF
lesson.summary: Factoring by GCF means dividing the greatest common factor out of every term and writing the polynomial as that factor times what remains, always checked by distributing back.
lesson.body:
Factoring by the greatest common factor combines two ideas you already have: finding a GCF, and the general meaning of factoring as writing an expression as a product. Once you know the GCF of a polynomial's terms, factoring by GCF simply means rewriting the polynomial as that GCF multiplied by whatever is left over in each term once the GCF has been divided out.

The process has three clear steps. First, find the GCF of every term in the polynomial. Second, divide each term by that GCF to see what remains. Third, write the original polynomial as the GCF multiplied by a parenthesis containing all those remaining pieces, in the same order as the original terms.

Take the polynomial 8x^3 + 12x^2 - 20x. Its GCF is 4x, since 4 is the largest number dividing 8, 12, and 20, and x is the lowest power of x present in all three terms. Dividing each term by 4x gives 8x^3 divided by 4x, which is 2x^2, then 12x^2 divided by 4x, which is 3x, then negative 20x divided by 4x, which is negative 5. Writing the GCF out front with the leftover terms in parentheses gives the factored form 4x(2x^2 + 3x - 5).

Always check factoring by distributing the GCF back across the parentheses, using the same distributive property that started this whole unit. Here, 4x times 2x^2 is 8x^3, 4x times 3x is 12x^2, and 4x times negative 5 is negative 20x. Adding these back together reproduces 8x^3 + 12x^2 - 20x exactly, confirming the factoring is correct. A second example shows the same idea with larger coefficients: for 9x^4 - 27x^3 + 18x^2, the GCF is 9x^2, since 9 divides 9, 27, and 18 evenly, and x^2 is the lowest power of x present. Dividing each term by 9x^2 gives x^2, negative 3x, and 2, so the factored form is 9x^2(x^2 - 3x + 2). Distributing 9x^2 back across x^2 - 3x + 2 gives 9x^4 - 27x^3 + 18x^2, matching the original exactly.

When the leading term of a polynomial is negative, it is standard practice to factor out a negative GCF so that the remaining polynomial starts with a positive term. For negative 3x^2 - 6x, the GCF is negative 3x rather than positive 3x. Dividing each term by negative 3x gives negative 3x^2 divided by negative 3x, which is x, and negative 6x divided by negative 3x, which is 2, so the factored form is negative 3x(x + 2). Distributing confirms it: negative 3x times x is negative 3x^2, and negative 3x times 2 is negative 6x, reproducing the original polynomial.

Factoring by GCF should be the very first thing you check on any polynomial, before trying any of the more specific techniques covered later in this unit, such as factoring trinomials, difference of squares, perfect square trinomials, or grouping. Pulling out a common factor first often shrinks the numbers involved and can reveal one of those other patterns hiding underneath, making the rest of the factoring much easier to spot.
